1:
When the psalm was written they answer differently. Calvin takes it for David's usual practice after deliverance — first the vows made in his difficulties, then his thanksgivings, to induce others to follow his example — and thinks he speaks of Saul's persecutions. Clarke lays out its shape in sections — prayer against treacherous enemies, then victory and songs of triumph, then a chorus of the people to their conquering king, and last the king's prayer for them — and refers it to the captivity, though some give it to David in his persecutions. Keil and Delitzsch add it as a third to the two psalms before it and place it in the persecution by Absalom, finding in it the intercession of the anointed one, himself in peril, for a people equally in need.

The rock draws the closest attention. Ellicott derives the Hebrew from a root implying to bind together, so the sense is not height but strength and solidity — Tyre, which bears the same name, being built on a broad shelf of rock — and observes that rock was a common metaphor for a tutelary deity. The Septuagint, apparently through timidity, suppresses it and renders simply my God. Clarke will not have the word confined even to that: it means not only my rock but my fountain, the origin of all the good I possess. Spurgeon makes it a resolve rather than a description: the immutable Jehovah is the immovable foundation of all our hopes; it will be vain to call to the rocks in the day of judgment, but our rock attends to our cries.

On the silence deprecated the readings run from grammar to protest. Ellicott prefers the Vulgate's be not silent from me, the word carrying, like its Greek counterpart, the double sense of deaf and dumb — turn not a deaf ear, or turn not from me in silence. Henry hears a man afraid of a God angry at his prayers, and asks two things in one petition: speak to me, with good and comfortable words, and speak for me, pleading my cause and commanding deliverances. Spurgeon presses the same distinction: formalists may be content without answers, but genuine suppliants need actual replies from heaven; God's voice is often so terrible that it shakes the wilderness, yet his silence is equally full of awe, and when he closes his ear we must cry the more earnestly. Clarke turns it into a charge against his own age: it is a modern refinement in theology which teaches that no man can know when God hears him.

Of the pit the notes are graver. Ellicott takes those who go down into it for the dead, or men about to die, and thinks the phrase suggests a bed of sickness. Henry says nothing can be so cutting to a gracious soul as the want of God's favour, and allows the harder reading, that this is the very misery of the damned, to whom God is ever silent. Calvin finds in the comparison a measure of David's straits, and hears him saying, I am nothing if thou leavest me; if thou succourest me not, I perish. It is not enough to be sensible of one's misery, he adds, unless a man, convinced he cannot help himself and renouncing all help from the world, betakes himself to God alone — which scarcely one in a hundred does, most having consciences so burdened that they gnaw the bit, or fill the air with complaints, or give way to despair. Gill hears the same singularity in the cry, a resolution to continue in prayer and direct it to the Lord only. Augustine hears another voice: it is the Mediator himself, strong of hand in the conflict of the Passion, praying that the eternity of the Word may not be severed from that which as Man he is.
2:
The lifted hands and the place they are lifted toward come first. Clarke says the word rendered oracle properly means the place in the holy of holies from which God answered the high priest, takes it for presumptive proof that a temple was then standing, and finds here the custom of stretching the hands towards it from a distance. Wesley says the same in a line, the holy of holies being where the ark was. Ellicott prefers the margin — the shrine, or the oracle, of thy sanctuary — and notes that the Hebrew word, of doubtful derivation, occurs nowhere else outside Kings and Chronicles; for the custom itself he sends the reader to Moses spreading his hands abroad and to Solomon at the dedication, and quotes Tennyson on those who, knowing God, lift not hands of prayer. Gill looks at what is lifted: supplications from the Spirit of grace, put up humbly under a sense of wants and unworthiness, on the footing of mercy rather than merit.

On the plea not to be drawn away the versions sharpen the verb. Ellicott would render it drag me not, pointing to the vision in Ezekiel where wicked nations are dragged down to destruction; Wesley has it plainly, drag me not, as thou dost these, to execution; Clarke asks only not to share the punishment of the wicked. Gill opens the request three ways — that God would not suffer him to be drawn aside, or give him into hands that would not spare him, or let him die the death of the wicked. Spurgeon supplies the picture the verb wants: they shall be dragged off like felons drawn on a hurdle to Tyburn, like logs to the fire, and David fears to be bound up in their bundle. The best of the wicked, he adds, are dangerous company in time and would make terrible companions for eternity.

Of those who speak peace with mischief in the heart Spurgeon writes at length. They have learned the manners of the place they are going to, lying being their conversation on the road; soft words, oily with pretended love, are the meshes of the infernal net in which Satan catches the precious life, and his children fish with their father's nets almost as cunningly. It is a sure sign of baseness when tongue and heart do not ring to the same note. Deceitful men are more to be dreaded than wild beasts — it were better to be shut up in a pit with serpents than compelled to live with liars — and he who cries peace too loudly means to sell it if he can get his price.

The imprecation Ellicott defends before the rest explain it. The justice of the lex talionis was deeply impressed on the mind of Israel, and there is no indication here of personal animosity: the poet, even where he speaks his own feelings, is identified with devout Israel, to whom it was natural to expect the judgment that alone could remove conditions unfavourable to true religion. Clarke reads the words as prediction rather than petition; Gill measures the deeds by their demerit, which is death eternal. On the regarding that is wanting, Gill lists the works ignored — creation, providence, redemption, and the Spirit's work upon the soul — and reports the Chaldee, that they do not understand the law of the Lord; Wesley limits it to God's providential works towards his people; Ellicott takes it of his even-handed justice, which the wicked forget or ignore, and hears Jeremiah's style in the contrast of building up and pulling down. Clarke finds a prophecy literally fulfilled: Babylon was destroyed by Cyrus and never built again, the Persian empire founded on its ruins. Keil and Delitzsch mark the hinge here, the first half of the psalm praying for deliverance and judgment and the second giving thanks for both.
6:
What it means to bless God at all Gill settles before anything else. It cannot be invoking a blessing on him, nor conferring one, neither of which a creature can do; nor does he need any, being God all-sufficient, God over all, blessed for ever. It is rather the ascribing of all blessedness to him, and the giving of praise and glory for mercies received. Spurgeon makes the same point from the other side: saints are full of benedictions, being a blessed people and a blessing people, but they give their best blessings, the fat of their sacrifices, to their glorious Lord.

That the psalm turns here from prayer to praise all of them notice, and one of them is troubled by it. Henry marks how soon the saints' sorrows are turned into songs and their prayers into praises: it was in faith that David prayed, and by the same faith he now gives thanks; those who pray in faith may rejoice in hope, being as sure of a real answer as if they had it already — and what we win by prayer we must wear by praise. Spurgeon says they who pray well will soon praise well, prayer and praise being the two lips of the soul, two angels climbing Jacob's ladder, two young roes that are twins feeding upon the mountain of myrrh. Real praise, he adds, is not irrational emotion but rises like a pure spring from the deeps of experience; and we should shun ingratitude and live daily in the heavenly atmosphere of thankful love. Ellicott finds the burst discordant with the rhythm as well as with the sense of the rest, and reports the explanations offered — that an interval elapsed and the writer took up his pen to record the answer, that the psalm is two pieces joined, or that this verse is an interpolation.

On the strength and the shield the notes gather round dependence. Gill takes the Lord for the author of both natural and spiritual strength, who gave David body and mind to bear up under all his exercises, and who would be the strength of his heart in the hour of death, when heart and strength fail. Henry hears in it a settled choice — my strength, to support me and carry me through all my services and sufferings; my shield, to protect me from all the malicious designs of my enemies; I have always found him so, and I expect he will still be so. Spurgeon calls it an act of appropriating faith by which the Psalmist takes the omnipotence of Jehovah to be his own, and observes that dependence upon the invisible God gives great independence of spirit, inspiring a confidence more than human. Clarke reduces the whole to a persuasion: that God hears, will answer, and will save.

The help spoken of as already had is what the rest explain. Wesley says David speaks of it as past because God had assured him by his Spirit that he had heard and accepted his prayers. Henry finds a double benefit in the trusting itself: God in due time gave the help trusted for, but the very trusting helped him meanwhile and kept him from fainting, the actings of faith being present aids to a drooping spirit and often helping it at a dead lift. The joy that follows he seats in the heart, whereas in the laughter of the fool the heart is sorrowful; and he takes the song for a debt discharged, since by it others are encouraged to trust in God too. Ellicott would render the rejoicing more strongly, danceth for joy, as the Prayer Book has it; on the last clause he notes that the Hebrew is literally from my song, that the reading is doubtful, and that the Septuagint's my flesh has flourished is probably correct.
8:
Whose strength the Lord is here turns on a single Hebrew word, and Clarke would change it. Instead of the form meaning to them, eight manuscripts of Kennicott and De Rossi read to his people, a reading confirmed by the Septuagint, the Syriac, the Vulgate, the Ethiopic, the Arabic and the Anglo-Saxon; it makes the passage more precise, and of its truth he thinks there can be no reasonable doubt — king and people alike being protected, upheld and saved by him. Ellicott reaches the same sense without the emendation: the strength meant is his people's, who are throughout in the poet's thought even where the individual and not the community speaks. For the second phrase he prefers the margin, stronghold of salvation. Gill simply carries the pronoun back, the Lord being the strength not of David only but of all his.

The turn outward at the close is what the rest fasten on. Gill observes the shape of the whole: the psalmist begins with petitions for himself and ends with prayers for the church — chosen, taken into covenant, given to the Son, and for whose sake Christ was appointed and sent as Saviour — so that this is a prayer of faith, as are the petitions following. Spurgeon calls it a prayer for the church militant, written in short words but full of weighty meaning, and insists we must pray for the whole church and not for ourselves alone. He finds a plea hidden in the words thy people, God's interest in his own portion leading him to guard it from destruction.

Each petition they take in turn. To save, for Spurgeon, is to deliver them from their enemies, preserve them from their sins, succour them under their troubles, rescue them from their temptations and ward off from them every ill; Clarke asks that they be kept from all their enemies, from idolatry, and from sin of every kind. To bless the inheritance Spurgeon reads as the granting of positive good — peace, plenty, prosperity, happiness — and as a prayer to revive, refresh, enlarge and sanctify the church; Clarke puts the ground of it in the mutual choice, that they have taken God for their God and he has taken them for his people. On feeding, Clarke notes that the Hebrew verb signifies both to feed and to govern, so that the request is at once to feed them as a shepherd does his flock and to rule them as a father does his children; Spurgeon asks that their bodily and spiritual wants be plentifully supplied, and that by word and ordinance God would direct, rule, sustain and satisfy the sheep of his hand.

On the last petition Clarke rises to the occasion. Lift them up for ever means maintain thy true Church and let no enemy prevail against it, preserve and magnify them for ever; and he sets the two eternities against each other — as hell is the bottomless pit in which damned spirits sink down for ever, or, as Chaucer says, downe all downe, so heaven is an endless height of glory in which there is an eternal rising and exaltation. Down, all down; up, all up; for ever and ever. Spurgeon keeps the same image nearer at hand: carry them in thine arms on earth, and then lift them into thy bosom in heaven, elevating their minds and thoughts, spiritualising their affections, making them heavenly, Christlike and full of God. Ellicott closes with the history of the words, which invite comparison with the shepherd of Isaiah who carries the lambs in his bosom, and notes that the incorporation of this petition into the Te Deum is one of those interesting facts that link Christian worship with the Jewish.
